knownFor.label: Persian carpets
knownFor.note: Silk and wool carpets made in royal workshops.

location.value: Iran and surrounding lands: at its height it included Azerbaijan, Armenia, eastern Georgia, Iraq and parts of Turkey, Afghanistan, Pakistan and Central Asia.

terrain.value: The Iranian plateau with surrounding mountains and deserts, the Caucasus, and the Persian Gulf coast.

climate.value: Arid to semi-arid, with underground irrigation channels (qanats).

resources.value: Silk (the main export), carpets, agriculture, and horses.

disasters.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

urbanisation.value: Capitals at Tabriz (1501–1555), Qazvin (1555–1598) and Isfahan (1598–1736), which became one of the great cities of its time.

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: Abbas I resettled Armenians (to New Julfa in Isfahan) and Georgians and Circassians. Slave-soldiers (gholams) from the Caucasus became a major force.

economicBase.value: Agriculture and taxation, with sharecropping. A revived Silk Road trade, with silk as the chief export.

tradeRoutes.value: An economic hub between East and West. English and Dutch companies traded in the Gulf after Hormuz was retaken from Portugal (1622).

wealth.value: No GDP estimate exists. It was prosperous under Abbas I. Decline came in the late 17th century, partly due to competition from Bengal silk.

moneyAndTax.value: Tuman and abbasi coins (1 tuman = 50 abbasi). Abbas I turned many provinces into crown lands to increase royal revenue.

inequality.value: Shah, Qizilbash tribal nobles, Persian bureaucrats, merchants and peasants. Slave-soldiers and forced labour.

governmentType.value: A monarchy under a near-absolute Shah with a grand vizier and Council of State. Officially called the “Guarded Domains of Iran”.

keyRulers.value: Ismail I (1501–1524, founder). Tahmasp I (1524–1576). Abbas I the Great (1588–1629). Sultan Husayn (1694–1722). Abbas III (1732–1736, last).

succession.value: Hereditary within the dynasty, often violent: princes were blinded or killed, and Qizilbash factions fought over succession.

institutions.value: Twelver Shiʿa Islam as state religion, Islamic and customary law, crown provinces, and the gholam slave-soldier corps (the “Third Force”).

stability.value: Qizilbash civil strife in the 16th century. Abbas I restored central control. Weakness after 1666 led to collapse in 1722.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between the Qizilbash Turkoman tribes, Persian administrators and the Caucasian gholams.

armyAndTech.value: Qizilbash cavalry, then Abbas I’s gunpowder infantry and artillery. One of the Islamic “gunpowder empires”.

majorWars.value: Defeat by the Ottomans at Chaldiran (1514). Long Ottoman–Safavid wars. Abbas I’s recapture of Bahrain (1602) and Hormuz (1622). The Afghan (Hotak) invasion and the fall of Isfahan (1722).

territoryChange.value: About 2.9 million km² in 1630 (Wikipedia infobox). Lost Iraq to the Ottomans in 1639 (Treaty of Zuhab).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals were the Ottoman Empire, the Uzbeks and the Mughals (over Kandahar). It sought European alliances against the Ottomans.

inventions.value: Gunpowder weapons, carpet weaving, ceramic tilework, and urban planning (Isfahan’s Naqsh-e Jahan Square).

scienceEducation.value: The Isfahan School of philosophy (Mulla Sadra, Mir Damad). Madrasas. Medicine relied mostly on older works.

openness.value: Hosted European envoys, merchants and missionaries, and Armenian traders. It imposed religious uniformity on Muslims (Shiʿism).

religion.value: Ismail I made Twelver Shiʿism the official religion, a major turning point in Islamic history that still shapes Iran today.

languageWriting.value: Persian (official), with Azerbaijani Turkic at court and in the army, plus Georgian, Armenian and others.

artsArchitecture.value: Isfahan’s mosques and palaces (Shah Mosque, Ali Qapu), illustrated Shahnameh manuscripts, the painter Reza Abbasi, and carpets.

socialStructure.value: Shah, tribal and court elites, ulama, merchants, peasants, and slave-soldiers.

sharedIdentity.value: Often considered the beginning of modern Iranian history: the first native dynasty since the Buyids to found a state officially known as Iran, unified by Shiʿism.

neighbours.value: The Ottoman Empire, the Mughal Empire, the Uzbek khanates, Georgia and Russia, and the Portuguese, English and Dutch in the Gulf.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Shiʿism within Iran and influenced Shiʿa communities in the Deccan and Iraq.

colonisation.value: Not a coloniser. It ruled neighbouring regions, especially in the Caucasus.

riseSignals.value: The Safaviyya Sufi order, the loyalty of Qizilbash warriors, and Ismail I’s conquests (1501).

peakPeriod.value: The reign of Abbas I the Great (1588–1629).

declineSignals.value: Weak later shahs, economic decline in the late 17th century, and military neglect.

outcome.value: Collapse. Afghan Hotak forces took Isfahan in 1722. After a restoration under Nader Shah’s control, the last shah was deposed in 1736 and the Afsharid dynasty followed.

sources.value: Persian court chronicles, European travellers and company records, and monuments. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026 (only the opening part was read word for word). See also Newman (2006).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. The end date is debated: 1722 (fall of Isfahan) or 1736 (last shah). Population is a rough estimate.
